One-line verdict: climate change policy analysts are not just writing reports; they research and analyse policy developments related to climate change, propose climate-related recommendations for action such as legislation and awareness-raising activities and fundraising methods, and are accountable for the research basis and the boundaries of their conclusions; O*NET defines the occupation as researching and analysing policy developments related to climate change and providing climate-related recommendations for action such as legislation and awareness-raising activities or fundraising methods.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to spend long hours reading literature and data and turn it into points decision-makers can use, and you can present and answer questions in public; the O*NET Work Context fields show that 91% use email every day, 77% hold face-to-face discussions every day, 64% have telephone conversations every day, 83% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day, 57% sit more than half the time, 52% consider working with a work group or team extremely important, and 57% consider coordinating or leading others very important.

Climate change policy analyst work falls into three connected but independent work surfaces. The first is research and analysis: collecting and reviewing climate-related research from government agencies and laboratories and other organisations, analysing and distilling climate-related research conclusions to provide to legislators and regulatory agencies and other stakeholders, studying the policies and practices and procedures of climate or environmental management, and analysing the analytical support needs of policy briefs on renewable energy and energy efficiency and climate change. The second is recommendation and communication: proposing legislative recommendations for climate or environmental management, proposing new or revised policies involving traditional and alternative fuel use and freight transport and other climate-related factors, writing research reports and memoranda and briefs and testimony and other written material, presenting climate-related information at public interest and government or other meetings, reviewing existing policy or legislation to identify environmental impacts, and writing reports or academic papers to communicate findings of climate-related research. The third is programme and resource advocacy: advocating that governments or environmental groups take action to mitigate climate change, developing or helping to develop education or outreach programmes on the environment or climate change, presenting and defending proposals for climate change research projects, and preparing grant applications to obtain funding for projects related to climate change or environmental management or sustainability.

Six recurring occupational judgements: whether the issue and the client's needs are clearly defined; whether the sources and basis of the material and data are reliable; whether the assumptions and uncertainties are written out; whether the recommendations assess impacts and costs and distributional effects; whether the wording distinguishes research conclusions from organisational positions; and whether the basis and versions are traceable.
Judgement one: are the issue and the client's needs clearly defined

First confirm the policy question and the decision setting and the time window and the required form of output, write the problem as a one-page problem statement and have the client confirm it before starting.
Judgement two: are the sources and basis of the material and data reliable
Prefer official statistics and peer-reviewed research and formal legal texts, and record the source and year and basis and units; for second-hand accounts, trace back to the original first.
Judgement three: are the assumptions and uncertainties written out
Write the key assumptions and scenarios and sensitivity analysis into the material, and state the conditions under which the conclusion does not hold, rather than giving only a single number.
Judgement four: do the recommendations assess impacts and costs and distributional effects

For each alternative, assess implementation cost and fiscal and regulatory feasibility and the effects on different groups, and state the trade-offs in the recommendation rather than presenting only the benefits.
Judgement five: does the wording distinguish research conclusions from organisational positions
In written and oral statements, distinguish conclusions of research findings from the position of the organisation or client, and obtain authorisation for external statements through the process.
Judgement six: are the basis and versions traceable
Archive the data and sources and calculation process and versions and reasons for revision, so that others can review the conclusion and understand the reason for each revision.

The six directions share part of their skills with this occupation: understanding environmental and climate issues, data and literature analysis, cross-department communication, and written and oral expression. The real differences lie in the nature of the duties and the form of output: the strategy and management direction is responsible for organisational commitments and programme delivery, the technical directions are responsible for the professional implementation of water resources and sites and environmental monitoring, and the compliance and enforcement direction is responsible for verification and penalty procedures, while this occupation centres on policy research and recommendations and writing material and is accountable for the analytical basis and uncertainty. When choosing, it is better to first validate with one deliverable policy brief than to compare names.

Policy and evidence analysis skills transfer, but each direction's authorisation and responsibility system must be obtained afresh.

entries.answer: Day-to-day work centres on literature and data research and policy analysis and recommendations and written and oral communication: collecting and reviewing climate-related research from government agencies and laboratories and other organisations, analysing and distilling research conclusions, studying and reviewing current policy and regulations, writing research reports and briefs and testimony, presenting and defending at meetings and in public, promoting mitigation action and education and outreach, and preparing grant applications. The O*NET Work Context fields show that 91% use email every day, 77% hold face-to-face discussions every day, 64% have telephone conversations every day, 83% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day, and 57% sit continuously or almost continuously.
entries.question: What do climate change policy analysts do every day?

entries.answer: Chief sustainability officers are responsible for organisational strategy and external commitments; water resource specialists do water resource technical analysis; brownfield redevelopment specialists are responsible for contaminated site assessment and remediation; environmental compliance inspectors are responsible for compliance verification and enforcement; sustainability specialists promote in-house programme delivery; environmental scientists and specialists carry out environmental science research; this occupation centres on climate change related policy research and recommendations and is accountable for the analytical basis. Shared skills do not mean the roles are interchangeable: the nature of the duties, the authority and the form of output differ.

entries.answer: The earlier-affected stages are those that can be structured and automated: literature searching and abstract summarising, statistical tidying and chart generation, initial policy text comparison, and brief and question-and-answer drafts. The later-affected stages are those requiring judgement and accountability: research design and choice of basis, causal and uncertainty judgements, weighing the feasibility and distributional effects of recommendations, and external statements and commitments.
entries.question: Which tasks are most easily automated?

entries.answer: Designing verifiable research questions, judging whether data bases are comparable, honestly stating uncertainty when evidence is insufficient, assessing the feasibility and distributional effects of recommendations, and making external statements within the scope of authority. These skills depend on professional training and the assumption of responsibility.

description.text: Climate change policy analysts research and analyse climate-related policy and make recommendations for legislative and awareness-raising and fundraising action, centring on research and analysis, policy recommendations and communication, and programme and funding advocacy: tasks and work context, the US wage and employment basis shown on the O*NET page (the parent occupation basis is marked), the mainland China statistical gap, the entry and qualification pathway, risks and exercises, all in one view.

subject.name: Climate change policy analysts
subject.summary: Research and analyse climate change related policy developments and make climate-related recommendations for action such as legislation and awareness-raising activities or fundraising methods: collect and review research and regulations and data, analyse and distil research conclusions, write research reports and briefs and testimony, present and defend at meetings and in public, promote mitigation action and education and outreach, and prepare grant applications to obtain funding for projects.
